clue.text: Garment for Wayneee and Terryyy?

parts.note: John Wayne and John Terry are two men called John; stretching their surnames with extra letters makes them long, so these are drawn-out Johns, and the phrase also names warm underwear

explanation.surface: A puzzling question about what clothing would suit two oddly spelt people called Wayne and Terry.
explanation.walkthrough: The stretched spellings matter: both men share the first name John (the actor John Wayne, the footballer John Terry), and their names have been made long.
explanation.definitionFit: Long underwear covering the legs is known by this plural name, so it is a garment.

clue.text: Broad collar, gold catches

indicators.note: the run of words collar, gold catches and holds the letters within it, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: A wide collar is snagged by golden fastenings, like a description of a showy costume.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the direction for a slow, stately and broad tempo is this Italian term, literally meaning wide.

clue.text: Dinks on knots designed to avoid slips

indicators.note: to knot something is to tangle and twist it, so the letters of dinks on are jumbled

explanation.surface: Little shots in a game are knotted together, apparently to stop anyone slipping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knots' looks like a noun after 'on', but it is a verb meaning tangles, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A surface or tyre built to stop sliding has a grip-giving finish described with this adjective.

clue.text: Very merry

definitions.meaning: in informal British speech the word can be an intensifier, as in '... good', meaning extremely
cheerful and full of good humour, a synonym for happy

explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb in British English it means extremely; as an adjective it means cheerful and festive.

clue.text: School leader, male, wise character standing to welcome first of boarders

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a male

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other
in a down entry, standing means the word is set upright, read from bottom to top

parts.note: Yoda is the wise Jedi master in Star Wars

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of boarders is used

explanation.surface: A head teacher figure, male and wise, stands to greet arriving boarding pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: The wise character is the Star Wars Jedi master; in a down entry 'standing' turns him upright, bottom to top, before he takes in the boarder's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools the senior pupil chosen to lead and represent the boys holds this title.

clue.text: Such twinkling remote around the black stuff

indicators.note: around means the word for remote is placed round the black stuff

parts.note: a remote chance is a slight one
tar is the sticky black stuff used on roads

explanation.surface: Describing a distant gleam around something dark, like tar or a night sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remote' means slim, as in a remote chance, not far away; 'the black stuff' is road tar.
explanation.definitionFit: The twinkling of far-off suns seen from Earth at night is exactly this kind of glow.

clue.text: Food, hot beef sandwiches

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to hold it between two layers, so the beef word encloses the hot letter

parts.note: a cow is the animal that gives beef
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A menu note: food here means hot beef sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' reads as a noun on a menu but is a verb: COW holds H.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal slang for grub or a meal, from Chinese pidgin, is this four-letter word.

clue.text: Actor wasting ton at end of one trip — on another?

indicators.note: wasting means the letters of ton are lost from the end of the dance, which then goes on to another

parts.note: to trip is to dance lightly, so one trip is a dance; the Charleston is a 1920s dance
taken as written
going on another trip means taking another dance, so the plain word for one replaces what was lost

explanation.surface: An actor wastes a ton of something at the end of one journey, and sets off on another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' is not a journey but a dance step: the Charleston loses TON from its end and goes on to another trip, a DANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dance is an English film and television actor, known for Game of Thrones.

clue.text: Exaggerate rubbish in old poem

indicators.note: in means the rubbish word goes inside the poem word

parts.note: verse is poetry, a poem
tat is cheap rubbishy goods

explanation.surface: Someone overstates the case by calling an old poem rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: To exaggerate is to state something too strongly, to make more of it than it is.

clue.text: Material cut, the lot turned back

parts.note: to prune is to cut back

indicators.note: turned back means the word for the lot is read backwards

parts.note: the lot means all of it

explanation.surface: Fabric was cut and the whole lot sent back.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong worsted fabric once used for gowns and shoe uppers carries this name, so it is a material.

clue.text: Walls of Alcatraz, behind which a meadow plant

indicators.note: behind which means the next pieces come after the walls
the walls of a word are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: a lea is a poetic word for a meadow

explanation.surface: Behind the walls of the prison island, a plant grows in a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walls of Alcatraz' gives A and Z, its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A flowering shrub related to the rhododendron is one example of a plant.

clue.text: Saboteur, important bird poking my darling up the Eiffel Tower?

indicators.note: poking means pushing into, so these words go inside the French phrase

parts.words: my darling up the Eiffel Tower
parts.note: up the Eiffel Tower means in France, where my darling is mon cher
key means crucial, important
a wren is a small bird

explanation.surface: A saboteur pokes an important bird at a lover on top of the Eiffel Tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up the Eiffel Tower' turns 'my darling' into French, MON CHER, which then holds KEY and WREN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who throws a spanner in the works, especially an eco-saboteur, is called this, after Edward Abbey's novel.

clue.text: Best sell screws, as trousers falling down?

indicators.note: to screw something up is to twist and mangle it, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sales pitch: the best-selling screws, perhaps for holding up trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screws' looks like the product being sold but is a verb, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers drop when nothing holds them at the waist, as when a strap is missing.

clue.text: Investigators tucked in to perfect cold tart

indicators.note: tucked in to means placed inside the word for perfect

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, perfect, written AI
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Detectives eat heartily into a perfectly chilled tart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucked in to' suggests eating and 'tart' a pastry; perfect is A1, written with the letter I for the digit.
explanation.definitionFit: Tart in its adjective sense means sharp or sour-tasting, like lemon juice.

clue.text: Drawl finally nailed by actor, not bad voice

indicators.note: nailed by means held fast by, so the letter sits inside the scrambled pieces
bad suggests something gone wrong, so the letters of actor and not are jumbled
finally means only the last letter of drawl is used

explanation.surface: An actor's drawling delivery is nailed, and the voice is not at all bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not bad' reads as praise, but 'not' is fodder and 'bad' the anagram signal; 'nailed by' means held inside the scrambled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest female singing range, and a singer with it, is a type of voice.

clue.text: Smash up the cars on street to check for their roadworthiness

indicators.note: smashing something up breaks it into pieces, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Smash the cars on the street to check whether they're fit for the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Vehicles are deliberately collided under test conditions to assess their safety, a check of fitness for use.

clue.text: European capital not entirely behind revolutionary bloke, a very old European

indicators.note: behind means the shortened capital comes after the turned word
revolutionary means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a guy is a bloke, a man

indicators.note: not entirely means the capital loses its last letter

parts.note: Oslo is the capital of Norway

explanation.surface: A European capital sits behind a revolutionary man, a very old European.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'European' belongs to the wordplay with 'capital'; the definition is the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of the former Balkan federation, dissolved in the 1990s, is an old European.

clue.text: Coming up, floating

definitions.meaning: something about to happen, rumoured and imminent
held aloft, airborne rather than on the ground

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means imminent or rumoured, as in change is about, and literally aloft above the ground.

clue.text: Aggressive invader gripping with good arm

indicators.note: gripping means holding, so the invader word goes round the other pieces

parts.note: the Huns were warlike invaders of Europe
and means together with

explanation.surface: An aggressive invader grips with a good arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arm' looks like a limb, but it means a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm is a weapon, and a pistol held in one hand is one.

clue.text: Welsh food, peculiar taste

parts.note: something rare is unusual, peculiar
a bit is a small taste, a morsel

explanation.surface: Welsh cuisine described as having a peculiar taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rabbit or rarebit is cheese melted on toast, a dish named after Wales.

clue.text: Tool in hand, phone line's cut

indicators.note: the line is cut into the phone letters, so it sits inside them

parts.note: TEL is the abbreviation for telephone
a row is a line, and 's here reads as is

explanation.surface: Holding a tool, someone finds the phone line has been cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' is not damage to the line: ROW cuts into TEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hand-held tool with a flat blade or scoop is used for gardening or plastering.

clue.text: Lower so very high?

parts.note: a lower is a cow, one that lows or moos; in the nursery rhyme the cow jumped very high, clearing the lunar disc, and the phrase also means delighted

explanation.surface: Asking whether something lowered could be so very high, which sounds contradictory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' is not the opposite of higher but one who lows: the cow of 'Hey Diddle Diddle', which leapt across the night sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means extremely happy, very high in spirits, echoing the nursery rhyme cow's leap.

clue.text: See 10
Cook too much food, revolting part sent back

indicators.note: sent back means the portion is read backwards
part means only a portion of the run food, revolting is used

explanation.surface: A diner sends back food that was cooked too long, part of it revolting.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcook is to leave something on the heat too long, spoiling it.

clue.text: He'll be leaving home next year with no degrees

definitions.text: He'll be leaving home next year

parts.note: O stands for nought, nothing, no
BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: Someone is about to move out next year without any qualifications.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared in 2016, when the US President's term would end in January 2017 and he would leave the White House.
explanation.definitionFit: The 44th US President was due to vacate the White House, his official home, the following year.

clue.text: See 6
Badger epidemic

definitions.meaning: to badger is to pester or harass
a widespread outbreak of disease, a pestilence

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to pester someone persistently; as a noun it is a deadly contagious disease.

clue.text: Reptile smart as a peacock?

parts.note: a boa is a large constricting snake, a reptile
to smart is to sting with pain

explanation.surface: A reptile, as smart as a peacock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart' suggests well-dressed, but it is the verb meaning to hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A peacock displaying its tail is the classic image of showing off and bragging.

clue.text: See 20
End of August, then a year in Provence? About time for a chat

indicators.note: end of means only the last letter of August is used
about means the French phrase goes around the letter for time

parts.note: the joke is that a year in sunny southern France is summer to summer, in French ete a ete

explanation.surface: After August ends, a year in southern France, about time for a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' wraps ETE A ETE around T, giving ETEATETE after the T from August.
explanation.definitionFit: A private conversation between two people is called by this French phrase, literally head to head.
